name: Tool Interface Design
question: Will the model use this tool well?
summary: A tool’s name, description, parameters, results and errors are a prompt the model reads every turn. Good design consolidates several API calls into one task-shaped tool, names parameters without ambiguity, returns only high-signal fields, and turns errors into instructions the model can act on. Measure it on a task set, like any prompt.
useCases: Agents with many overlapping tools that pick the wrong one
Tools that return large raw records or opaque error codes
Wrapping an existing API for use by agents

items.detail: by far the most important factor; 3–4 sentences or more
one schedule_event instead of list_users + list_events + create_event
unambiguous names (user_id, not user), enums, defaults
semantic fields, pagination and a concise response_format
say what was wrong and how to fix it
load definitions on demand with tool search past roughly 30–50 tools

steps: Start from real tasks and merge chains of thin endpoints into task-shaped tools
Write descriptions: what it does, when to use it, when not to, and caveats
Trim results to the fields the next step needs; add pagination and a concise mode
Return actionable errors, then evaluate on a task set and read the wrong-choice transcripts
pitfalls: Near-duplicate tools (search_txn, find_transaction) split the model’s choices
Raw payloads fill the context and bury the field that matters
Opaque codes such as E422 leave the model retrying blind
remember: Design tools for the model that reads them, not for the API behind them.
caption: Illustrative results on a 10-task set. Token counts echo Anthropic’s example of concise responses.

steps.title: Start from the task
steps.text: Booking needs one question answered: who is free, and when? One find_free_slot tool replaces four thin endpoints the model had to chain in the right order.

steps.title: Write the description
steps.text: Say what it does, when to use it, when not to, and what it returns. Anthropic calls the description by far the most important factor in tool performance.

steps.title: Make parameters unambiguous
steps.text: An enum for the department, a typed date with an example, and a default for response_format. The model cannot invent a department that does not exist.

steps.title: Return only what the next step needs
steps.text: The concise mode returns ids, names and free times, about 380 tokens instead of a 4,100-token roster record, and never more than 10 rows.

steps.title: Turn errors into instructions
steps.text: A past date gets a message that names the problem, the value sent and the fix. The model corrects the year in one retry instead of guessing.

steps.title: Evaluate on a task set
steps.text: Run real requests, score which tool was chosen and with which arguments, and read the wrong-choice transcripts. Tool design is prompt design, so measure it.

pros: Fewer wrong tool choices with the same model
Smaller results cut tokens and cost on every later turn
Actionable errors turn failures into one-step corrections
Task-shaped tools need fewer calls per task
cons: Consolidating tools takes design work and domain knowledge
Descriptions need maintenance when behaviour changes
Concise results can hide a field the model later needs
Gains must be measured on a task set, not assumed
avoidWhen: A single, obvious tool with one argument
A third-party server you cannot change: wrap it or choose another instead

playgroundGuide.scenario: A Pune hospital’s scheduling agent handles OPD bookings. Each booking task needs 3 correct tool calls. Every turn resends 1,500 tokens of instructions plus the tool definitions, and each tool result stays in the history for about 1.5 later turns. Input tokens cost ₹250 per million. A wrong tool choice costs one wasted call; a bad argument costs one or more retries.
controls: Drag the number of tools exposed, from 5 to 60.
Choose terse or full descriptions, raw or concise results, and bare or actionable errors.
Turn on tool search, which loads only 5 relevant tools per turn.

missions.text: Reach at least 95% right choices with 40 or more tools.
missions.hint: Full descriptions alone reach 88% at 40 tools. Load tools on demand so the model sees only a few at a time.

missions.text: Keep results under 500 tokens per call while holding at least 90% right choices.
missions.hint: Concise results, plus descriptions good enough to keep choices accurate.

missions.text: With all 60 tools, recover from a bad date in one retry and keep the cost under ₹5,000 per 1,000 tasks.
missions.hint: Three changes are needed: actionable errors, concise results and on-demand loading.

goals: Rewrite a set of thin endpoints as task-shaped tools
Explain why descriptions, result size and error text change accuracy and cost
Calculate the token cost of tool definitions and results per task

practice.scenario: A Pune hospital’s scheduling agent was given 30 thin EHR endpoints, such as list_doctors, get_roster, get_leaves and list_booked_slots. It often chained them wrongly and read whole roster records. The team replaced them with 8 task tools such as find_doctor_availability and book_opd_slot, with full descriptions, concise results and errors that say how to fix the input.

industries.use: OPD booking tools that already combine rosters, leave and booked slots
One search_transactions tool with filters instead of three overlapping search functions
Namespaced tools (crm_contacts_search, crm_deals_update) across several integrations

practice.analogy: A good form at a government office. It asks for exactly what the clerk needs, gives an example for each box, and says why a form was rejected, so you can fix it at the counter instead of starting again.

library.name: FastMCP
library.what: A Python framework for MCP servers: type hints become the input schema, the docstring becomes the description, and ToolError returns an actionable error.

practice.note: roster stands for your own EHR client. The same design rules apply to plain function-calling tools.

samples.code:
from datetime import date
from typing import Annotated, Literal
from fastmcp import FastMCP
from fastmcp.exceptions import ToolError

mcp = FastMCP("opd-scheduling")

@mcp.tool
def find_doctor_availability(
    department: Literal["cardiology", "orthopaedics", "paediatrics", "general_medicine"],
    on_date: Annotated[date, "Clinic date in ISO 8601, e.g. 2026-10-03"],
    response_format: Literal["concise", "detailed"] = "concise",
) -> list[dict]:
    """Find doctors with free OPD slots in one department on one date.
    Use this before book_opd_slot: it already combines the roster, leave and booked slots.
    Do not use it for a patient's existing appointments (use get_patient_appointments).
    Returns at most 10 doctors; 'concise' gives doctor_id, name and free slot times only."""
    today = date.today()
    if on_date < today:
        raise ToolError(f"on_date must be today ({today.isoformat()}) or later; "
                        f"you sent {on_date.isoformat()}. Check the year and try again.")
    rows = roster.free_slots(department, on_date)[:10]
    if response_format == "concise":
        return [{"doctor_id": r.id, "name": r.name, "free": r.slots} for r in rows]
    return [r.model_dump() for r in rows]

numericDrill.question: An agent exposes 40 tools, each with a 350-token definition, on every one of 6 turns. With tool search, each turn carries only a 500-token search tool plus the 5 tools it loads. How many definition tokens does one task save?

interview.question: How would you improve an agent that keeps choosing the wrong tool?
interview.answer: Read the transcripts where it chose wrongly. Usually tools overlap or descriptions are thin. Merge near-duplicates into one task-shaped tool, write descriptions that say what, when, when not and caveats, use unambiguous parameter names and enums, and load tools on demand when there are dozens. Then re-run a task set to confirm the fix.

interview.question: What makes a good tool result and a good tool error?
interview.answer: A result returns only high-signal, human-readable fields, with pagination, filters and a concise mode, because every token is read by the model. An error says what was wrong and how to fix it, for example the expected format and the value received, so the model can correct itself in one retry.

mistakes.mistake: Wrapping every API endpoint one-to-one as a tool
mistakes.fix: Design task-shaped tools that do what the user asked in one call

mistakes.mistake: Returning bare error codes such as E422
mistakes.fix: Say what was wrong, what was expected, and what was received

quiz.question: A support agent has search_txn, find_transaction and lookup_payment, and uses them interchangeably with poor results. What is the best first fix?
options: Add a fourth search tool for edge cases
Merge them into one search_transactions tool with clear filters and a full description
Remove all descriptions to save tokens
Force the model to call all three every time
quiz.explanation: Overlapping tools split the model’s choices; one task-shaped tool with a clear description removes the ambiguity.

quiz.question: According to Anthropic’s guidance, what is by far the most important factor in tool performance?
options: The length of the tool name
The output format of the model
quiz.explanation: Anthropic calls detailed descriptions by far the most important factor, aiming for 3–4 sentences or more.

quiz.question: A calendar agent must list users, list events and then create an event to book a meeting. What does good tool design suggest?
options: One schedule_event tool that finds availability and books
Add a fourth tool that calls the other three
quiz.explanation: Consolidate chains of thin calls into one task-shaped tool that does what the user asked.

quiz.question: A tool returns full 4,100-token product records when the next step needs only id, price and stock. With concise results of 380 tokens, and 3 calls per task, how many result tokens are saved per task?
A booking tool returns {"error": "E422"} when the date is in the past. What happens next, typically?
options: The model corrects the date immediately
The model retries blindly or gives up, because the code gives no hint
quiz.explanation: Opaque codes give the model nothing to act on; actionable errors let it correct itself in one retry.

quiz.question: Which make a parameter unambiguous? Select all that apply.
options: Naming it customer_id rather than user
Giving an example format for dates
quiz.explanation: Specific names, enums and examples remove ambiguity; a generic name such as data does the opposite.

quiz.question: An agent loads 60 tools on every turn and accuracy has dropped. What does Anthropic suggest past roughly 30–50 tools?
options: Load tool definitions on demand with tool search
Shorten every description to one word
quiz.explanation: Selection accuracy degrades with many tools; tool search loads only relevant definitions.

quiz.question: 40 tools of 350 definition tokens each are sent on each of 6 turns. With tool search, each turn carries a 500-token search tool plus 5 loaded tools. How many definition tokens are saved per task?
You connect tools from several services to one agent. Which help the model tell them apart? Select all that apply.
options: Descriptions that say when not to use a tool
quiz.explanation: Namespaces and explicit “when not to use” guidance separate similar tools; identical names or missing schemas add confusion.

quiz.question: Which error message best helps the model self-correct?
options: “pickup_date must be today or later; you sent 2025-10-03. Check the year.”
quiz.explanation: It names the rule, the value received and the fix.

quiz.question: Claude Code caps tool responses by default at about how many tokens?
quiz.explanation: Anthropic’s engineering post notes Claude Code restricts tool responses to 25,000 tokens by default.

quiz.question: An agent’s search tool returns long raw JSON with UUIDs. Which result changes help? Select all that apply.
options: Return human-readable names alongside or instead of opaque ids
Return every field so nothing is missed
quiz.explanation: Semantic fields, pagination and a concise mode make results high-signal. Returning everything floods the context.

quiz.question: How should you confirm a redesign of tool descriptions actually helped?
options: Ask the model which version it prefers
Run a task set, score tool choice and arguments, and read failing transcripts
quiz.explanation: Tool design is prompt design: evaluate it on realistic tasks before and after.

quiz.question: A tool definition averages 250 tokens. An agent exposes 32 tools on every turn of a 5-turn task. How many definition tokens per task?
Which are signs of poor tool design in agent transcripts? Select all that apply.
options: The model calls two tools that do almost the same thing in one task
The model retries the same bad argument several times
The model calls a tool once and answers
The model asks the user for a missing account number
quiz.explanation: Near-duplicate calls and blind retries point to overlapping tools and unhelpful errors. The other two are good behaviour.

quiz.question: Anthropic’s example cut a Slack-thread result from 206 tokens to 72 with a concise format. Roughly what fraction was removed?
In MCP, how should a tool report that an input failed validation, so the model can self-correct?
options: As a JSON-RPC protocol error only
As a tool execution error in the result, with isError true
quiz.explanation: MCP puts input-validation failures in tool execution errors (isError true) so the model can see and fix them.

quiz.question: A hospital replaces 30 thin EHR endpoints with 8 task tools. Which benefits should you expect? Select all that apply.
quiz.explanation: Task-shaped tools reduce calls, ambiguity and definition tokens, but nothing guarantees zero errors.

quiz.question: Which description is best for a refund tool?
options: “Refunds a settled UPI payment by UTR, up to the original amount. Use only after the dispute is approved; do not use for failed payments, which auto-reverse. Returns refund id and status.”
“Use this tool for everything related to money.”
quiz.explanation: It says what, when, when not and what it returns.

quiz.question: Which tools help you design and test tool interfaces? Select all that apply.
options: MCP Inspector, to call tools by hand and read raw results
promptfoo, to score tool choice across a task set
A CDN, to cache tool definitions
A load balancer, to spread tool calls
quiz.explanation: Inspector shows exactly what the model sees; promptfoo measures behaviour across tasks. The others are infrastructure.
